title: Tariff Surcharge Clawback for B2B Buyers
one_liner: A contingency-fee service that mines a buyer's 2025-26 supplier invoices for 'tariff surcharge' lines and recovers a share of the IEEPA refunds those suppliers are now collecting.
customer: Multi-unit restaurant and retail franchisees, contractor purchasing co-ops, and mid-market distributors' customers that paid itemized tariff, freight or 'inflation' surcharges to suppliers who were the importer of record. They pay a 20-30% success fee on money recovered.
problem: IEEPA duty refunds go only to the importer of record (IOR) or a party the IOR designates. Buyers who paid the tariff as a surcharge or a higher price get nothing unless they ask. AutoZone booked about $96M and Cracker Barrel $15M, with MillerKnoll $16.5M and Worthington $4M. Downstream buyers have no visibility into what their suppliers recovered and no process to ask for it.
solution: Read-only inbox and AP connectors pull 2025-26 invoices and extract surcharge, 'tariff', 'duty' and 'trade cost recovery' line items. The system estimates each supplier's IEEPA exposure from public import-manifest data. It checks the supplier's terms for pass-back language, such as 'surcharge will be removed or refunded if tariffs are rescinded'. It then generates a claim letter with an offer to accept credit memos or to have the supplier name the buyer as the CBP Form 4811 notify party so the refund routes to the buyer. A second module audits new diesel and fuel surcharges against the contract formula and the EIA diesel index. Claims are sent to the top 20 suppliers per buyer, and unclaimed money is tracked to closure.
why_now: CBP's CAPE portal opened in 2026 and is issuing refunds within 60-90 days of an accepted declaration. Refunds are landing in Q3-Q4 2026 P&Ls as one-time gains. Suppliers are least defensible in the first months after booking a windfall and will negotiate to keep customer goodwill. Diesel is $6.53/gal, up $2.78 year over year, so a wave of fresh surcharge invoices is arriving that nobody audits.
revenue_model: A 20-30% contingency fee on recovered refunds and credits, plus $199-$999/month for continuous surcharge auditing (fuel, energy, 'regulatory recovery' fees) once the first recovery lands.
non_obvious_insight: The refund windfall is a transfer from customers to importers, and the CFOs say so. AutoZone's CFO said 'the refund environment was deflationary, and the industry likely would have raised prices faster if both retailers and suppliers hadn't received cost relief' (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/22/autozone-azo-q4-2026-earnings-call-transcript/). Cracker Barrel booked a $15M refund and MillerKnoll $16.5M, worth 180 bps of gross margin (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/23/cracker-barrel-cbrl-q4-2026-earnings-call-transcript/ and https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/22/mlkn-q1-2027-earnings-call-transcript/). CBP states 'Only the IOR ... or the authorized customs broker ... may file' and never mentions downstream buyers, couriers or DDP shipments (https://www.cbp.gov/trade/programs-administration/trade-remedies/ieepa-duty-refunds). Every downstream claim is therefore a negotiation, and the buyer who holds the 2025 invoices has the leverage. Nobody is selling that to the buyer side. The legal caveat is that the buyer needs an explicit surcharge line or contract language to have a real claim, so the product should target only those cases.
first_30_days: Recruit 5-8 restaurant franchisee groups or contractor purchasing co-ops through franchisee associations and buying-group managers, with a free 'we only get paid if you get paid' offer. Export 2025 AP data or forward invoice PDFs, then have an analyst plus an LLM extraction script build a surcharge ledger for the top 15 suppliers each. Send the first 30 claim letters with a one-page template that cites the refund program and asks for credit or 4811 routing. Have a supply-chain lawyer review the template. Aim to close the first paid recovery within 60-75 days.
